**To: Owner**
**Subject: Customer Care Agent screening: both candidates qualify, plus a problem with the screening note**

I screened both applicants against the posted must-haves.

| | 1+ yr customer service | Fluent written and spoken English | Weekends | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Tomasz Nowak** | Yes, 3 years in a bank call center handling English-language calls | Written: clear and well written. Spoken: to confirm at phone screen, though 3 years of English-language calls is strong evidence | Yes | Meets all must-haves |
| **Hannah Price** | Yes, 2 years on a retail help desk | Written: clear and well written. Spoken: to confirm at phone screen | Yes | Meets all must-haves |

**Recommendation:** Advance both to a phone screen.

**Why I didn't use the hiring manager's note:** The note says to pass along only native English speakers. I can't apply it as written. Screening on native-speaker status is screening on national origin, and in practice it would exclude Tomasz because he grew up in Poland, even though he meets every posted requirement and has more relevant experience than Hannah. That exposes Brightwater to real discrimination liability under Title VII and similar state laws. It also isn't a good predictor of performance. The posting asks for fluent English, and fluency is a legitimate, testable requirement. Being a native speaker is not.

The concern behind the note, that callers can't understand the agent, is a legitimate business concern. It can be handled in a lawful way:
- Use a short live phone or video screen for every candidate, scored on the same job-related rubric: clarity, comprehension, pace, and handling a mock customer call.
- Judge whether a candidate can be easily understood by customers in the role. Having an accent is not a disqualifier by itself.
- Apply the same process to every candidate, and keep the notes.

**Suggested replacement for the screening note:**
"Advance candidates who meet the posted must-haves. Confirm spoken English fluency and clarity through a standard phone screen with a scored rubric applied to all candidates."

I haven't contacted the hiring manager or either candidate. If you'd like, I can forward the replacement note to the hiring manager, draft the phone screen rubric, and schedule both phone screens.

---

**Why I set the note aside**
- "Native English speaker" isn't the same as "fluent English." Many non-native speakers are fully fluent, and Tomasz has 3 years of direct experience handling English-language calls.

- Add a short phone or video screen for every finalist, with a role-play call scored on clarity, comprehension, and ability to resolve the issue.
- Use the same rubric for everyone, and record scores rather than impressions.

This tests what the job needs, and it will tell you more than a native-speaker rule would.

"We're screening on the posted requirements: 1+ years in customer service, fluent written and spoken English, and weekend availability. We can't screen on native-speaker status or accent, because it creates legal exposure for the company. To address caller clarity, we'll add a structured call-simulation round for all finalists, scored on comprehension and clarity. Both current applicants meet the requirements and are moving forward."
